newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwaiti men vote, women demand equality.
newsitem.headline: Kuwaiti men vote, women demand equality.

text.p: Kuwaiti men on Monday voted for the second parliament since the 1991 Gulf War while some 200 women held gatherings to demand political rights.
"Equality and justice" read a banner held by a group of female activists in front of a polling station to demand that Kuwaiti women be given a say in the country's affairs.
"Yes to equality no to discrimination," read another banner.
The 200 activist women held two separate gatherings of 100 each. They plan to hold a "silent march" later on Monday.

Kuwait is the only Gulf Arab state to hold parliamentary elections, but just one seventh of the population of 700,000 has the right to vote. Women, over 50 percent of Kuwaitis, cannot run for office or vote.
Kuwaiti women, the most liberal in a Moslem conservative area, run businesses, head diplomatic missions and help to steer the oil industry.

Analysts forecast that over 70 percent of the 107,000-strong electorate would vote. Polls opened at 8 a.m. (0500 GMT) for 12 hours. About 230 candidates, including 41 members of the outgoing parliament, are standing for the 50-seat assembly.
"The turnout is good so far," said an Interior Ministry official three hours after polls opened. He expects larger numbers to vote in the afternoon when employees get off work.
Parliament's political adviser Abdullah al-Shayeji told Reuters that security and the economy were the top issues in the election.

He said last month's tension between Washington and Baghdad and the October 1994 Iraqi buildup on the border showed Kuwaitis how vulnerable their small country was, pushing "genuine security concerns to the front burner".
Some of the new MPs are expected to press for further defence measures to deter Iraq, while also seeking stronger powers to monitor state spending and tackle alleged corruption.

The outgoing, opposition-dominated parliament was no rubber stamp. It opened probes into alleged official corruption and claims of poor government management before Iraq's 1990 invasion and occupation of Kuwait.

Incidents since the Gulf War have shown that Kuwait and most of its sparsely populated Gulf Arab allies, among the world's largest arms importers, will continue to depend on the United States and other Western powers.
Speaker Ahmad al-Saadoun said in his closing address on Saturday that parliament "has defended public funds and held accountable those who allowed themselves to violate its sanctuary."
Political analysts say in the 1992 election the government was still fresh out of the Gulf crisis and was not in total control to influence the outcome.
"Now it is playing the game very smoothly and can pick and choose," said Shayeji. The state has repeatedly stressed that its role in the election was purely organisational.

A Western diplomat said despite repeated allegations of vote-buying by pro-government and other candidates none of the leading politicians was questioning the fairness of the process or calling for international monitoring.
